fixes.explanation: Yes, friend, and the text says it right up front: “Then the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary, Hadad the Edomite, from the royal line of Edom.” Solomon is David's son and Israel's king, and Hadad is the first name on the trouble list. Royal line and all, he shows up like he's got an appointment. The LORD is the one who raised him up.

That's it. Verse 17 says Hadad was “…still just a young boy…” when he fled to Egypt, along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. Joab, the army's commander, had struck down every male in Edom, and yet Hadad is still around. A young boy on the run, and he's the one the LORD raises up against Solomon.

Good thinking, but the text never says Joab spared him or kept him as a prisoner. Verse 17 says Hadad, “…still just a young boy…” had fled to Egypt, along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. That's how the text tells us he's still alive.

That's the whole package. Verse 18 says Pharaoh “…gave Hadad a house and land and provided him with food.” Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. Hadad shows up with his men, and he gets a house, land and meals, which is a pretty strong welcome.

Pharaoh does take Hadad in, but no army post is in the text. Verse 18 says Pharaoh gave him a house and land and provided him with food. Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. A post in the army just isn't on that list.

No ship in this one, friend. Verse 18 says Pharaoh gave Hadad a house and land and provided him with food. Later Hadad says to Pharaoh, “Let me go, that I may return to my own country.” (1 Kings 11:21) Pharaoh, king of Egypt, answers with a question, not a ship.

True. Verse 20 says Genubath was weaned in Pharaoh's palace by Queen Tahpenes herself, and that he “…lived there among the sons of Pharaoh.” Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, and Genubath is Hadad's son. So Hadad's boy lived right there among the royal kids.

Master is the word. Rezon, son of Eliada, “…had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah…” (1 Kings 11:23) He gathered men to himself, and he ended up ruling over Aram with hostility toward Israel. So the second adversary starts out as a man on the run and ends up a ruler.

An ally? Rezon wasn't running to a friend, he was running from somebody. Verse 23 says he “…had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah…” (1 Kings 11:23) Nobody flees from a buddy, friend. The word is master.

True. Verse 26 says, “Jeroboam was a servant of Solomon, but he rebelled against the king…” Jeroboam son of Nebat is an Ephraimite from Zeredah, and his mother is a widow named Zeruah. So this trouble comes from one of Solomon's own servants.

Gezer doesn't come up here. Verse 28 says Solomon “…put him in charge of the whole labor force of the house of Joseph.” The text does mention Solomon building supporting terraces and repairing a gap in the wall of the city of his father David (1 Kings 11:27). But it never says Jeroboam worked on that wall. His job is the labor force of the house of Joseph.

No gift of a coat here. Ahijah the Shilonite, a prophet, took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and “…tore it into twelve pieces…” (1 Kings 11:30). Then he tells Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces for yourself…” (1 Kings 11:31). So the word is pieces, not a cloak on his shoulders.

The text says nothing about spreading the cloak out on the road. Ahijah the Shilonite, a prophet, took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and “…tore it into twelve pieces…” (1 Kings 11:30). Then he speaks for the LORD to Jeroboam. What Ahijah does with that cloak is tear it.

The word is bigger than cities. Ahijah says, “Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten tribes.” (1 Kings 11:31) He tore the cloak into twelve pieces and told Jeroboam to take ten, and the LORD names ten tribes. The promise is about tribes, not a list of towns.

Right. The LORD says, “But one tribe will remain for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.” (1 Kings 11:32) David is Israel's earlier king, and Jerusalem is where the LORD chose to put His Name (1 Kings 11:36). Two reasons, friend, and the LORD names both Himself.

The text says nothing about Jeroboam asking for mercy. The LORD says one tribe will remain “…for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.” (1 Kings 11:32) The reasons He gives here are David and Jerusalem.

No treaty is named by the LORD here. He says, “For they have forsaken Me to worship Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites.” (1 Kings 11:33) Egypt shows up in this passage, first with Hadad and then with Jeroboam. But the reason for the torn kingdom is the worship of other gods.

The LORD doesn't count it by anybody's age, friend. He says, “…I will not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon’s hand, because I have made him ruler all the days of his life for the sake of David My servant…” (1 Kings 11:34) All the days of his life is Solomon's timeline. Jeroboam's birthday isn't on that calendar.

Son is right. The LORD says, “But I will take ten tribes of the kingdom from the hand of his son and give them to you.” (1 Kings 11:35) Just before that, He said He would not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon's hand (1 Kings 11:34). The text names that son at the end of the passage (1 Kings 11:43).
False is right. The LORD tells Jeroboam that He will humble David's descendants, but not forever (1 Kings 11:39). The humbling has an end. That's the LORD's own word on it, friend.

No army in this part of the story. Verse 40 says Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, and “…Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt…” Solomon is Israel's king. Jeroboam fled, he didn't fight.

Yes. Jeroboam fled to Shishak king of Egypt, “…where he remained until the death of Solomon.” (1 Kings 11:40) He stays in Egypt until Solomon, Israel's king, is gone. The text sets his stay by Solomon's life, not by a number.

Hadad is one of the adversaries from earlier in this passage, but the text never names him as Solomon's successor. Verse 43 says Solomon “…rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.” The new king is Solomon's own son. That's the fact the text hands us.
